headline: Sound reveals India's hidden finless porpoises
meta_description: New acoustic monitoring reveals Indo-Pacific finless porpoises are four times more common in Indian waters than visual surveys suggested—offering hope for cons…
summary_short: Acoustic surveys detect finless porpoises four times more often than traditional visual methods, revealing how sound can unlock conservation for India's elusive cetacean…
body:
A 2025 study off the Sindhudurg coast north of Goa has fundamentally shifted how researchers understand India's finless porpoise populations. Using specialized sound-recording devices, scientists detected Indo-Pacific finless porpoises four times more frequently than conventional boat-based visual surveys—revealing that these small cetaceans are far more prevalent in Indian waters than previously believed. The discovery matters urgently: the shallow coastal zones where these porpoises live are becoming increasingly hazardous, with an estimated 26 animals dying annually as bycatch along a single 100-kilometer stretch of Goa's coastline. Entanglement in fishing nets is particularly lethal for porpoises, whose spade-shaped teeth snag easily in nets, unlike dolphins' conical teeth that sometimes allow escape. The shift toward acoustic monitoring offers genuine hope for long-term population tracking and protection.

The Indo-Pacific finless porpoise (Neophocaena phocaenoides) is built for stealth. Weighing only 30–45 kilograms and lacking a dorsal fin, it navigates murky, shallow waters by emitting high-frequency echolocation clicks unique to the species—far above human hearing but clearly audible to specialized equipment. These acoustic signatures provide what visual surveys cannot: reliable detection in the turbid, low-visibility conditions where these porpoises actually live.

But this invisible world is collapsing under industrial noise. Commercial engines, high-speed vessel traffic, and port activity are shattering the porpoises' acoustic landscape, impairing their ability to distinguish food from danger. Conservation now depends on understanding their true numbers—something only sound can reveal. By shifting from boats and binoculars to hydrophones and data, researchers are finally seeing porpoises the way the porpoises see themselves.
quick_facts: Acoustic surveys detected finless porpoises 4 times more often than visual surveys
Indo-Pacific finless porpoises weigh 30–45 kg and measure 1.5–1.9 meters long
Estimated 26 porpoises die annually as bycatch along 100 km of Goa coastline
Study conducted in 2025 off Sindhudurg coast, north of Goa state
Porpoises navigate using echolocation in turbid coastal waters
